**ID**: ADR-169
**Status**: Accepted — the FRAMES ablation (metaharness, n=50, seed 42, 2026-06-28) already complies; this ADR makes the discipline binding for every benchmark number ruflo publishes
**Date**: 2026-07-03
**Authors**: rUv (drafted with Claude Code)
**Related ADRs**:
- ADR-167 (GAIA submission integrity — audits a *submission* against exploit vectors)
- ADR-168 (GAIA harness evidence recording — makes the evidence *exist*)
- ADR-133/135/136 (GAIA harness, tracks, hardness routing)
**Source evidence**: FRAMES/GAIA ablation integrity self-audit vs the Berkeley RDI
vectors (`runs/summary.json`, scored by `score-gaia.mjs`) — every verdict below
was measured from committed artifacts, not asserted.

---

## 1. Context

ADR-167 and ADR-168 cover *earning* integrity: was the score obtained by
solving tasks, and is the evidence recorded. This ADR covers the third leg —
**reporting** integrity: given honestly-earned numbers, are they *presented*
in a way that survives the Berkeley RDI lens?

RDI's April 2026 study broke eight major benchmarks not only through harness
exploits but through **reporting artifacts that inflate scores without any
cheating in the run itself**: relaxed/substring metrics presented as accuracy
(normalization collisions), undisclosed best-of-N presented as single-attempt
scores, no-work passes hidden in aggregates, and unreproducible cherry-picked
runs.

The metaharness FRAMES ablation self-audit demonstrated that these vectors are
cheap to close *by construction* — and that the same discipline was already
implicitly present in the ablation's artifacts. What is missing is a binding
standard so future numbers (GAIA, FRAMES, terminal-bench, whatever comes next)
can't regress.

## 2. Decision

Every benchmark number ruflo publishes — README, release notes, leaderboard
submission, gist, blog — MUST satisfy five rules. `summary.json`-style scored
=== ADR-171 ===
# ADR-171: Provenance-Tiered Evaluation Oracle for Distillation Gold-Labeling

**ID**: ADR-171
**Status**: Proposed — implemented on `feat/agenticow-integration` (ships in 3.21.0)
**Date**: 2026-07-04
**Authors**: rUv (drafted with Claude Code)
**Related ADRs**:
- ADR-169 (Benchmark reporting integrity — never present a proxy as ground truth; this ADR is that principle applied to training-data labels)
- ADR-170 (agenticow substrate — supplies the branches whose promotion this oracle gates)
- ADR-172 (Fable advisor harness — the Tier-2 judge mechanism)
- ADR-173 (Remote GPU distillation — consumes the labels this oracle produces)

---

## 1. Context

The weight-eft distillation slice (ADR-173) needs a gold `resolved: boolean` per trajectory to build SFT data. **ruflo has no SWE-bench oracle** — historically `resolved` was derived from `output-verifier` structural confidence: a *proxy*. A tune on proxy-labeled data distills plausible-but-wrong completions, and a single blended "resolved" number is exactly the benchmark theater ADR-169 forbids.

Two facts changed the calculus:
- A real GPU/compute host (`ruvultra`, tailscale) can execute actual task evaluations (FAIL_TO_PASS), giving true ground truth for trajectories that carry a test spec.
- A headless Fable judge (ADR-172) is cost-viable (~$0.02/item batched) as a smarter-than-structural labeler for the residue.

## 2. Decision

Label `resolved` through a **tiered trust hierarchy**, and **tag every label with its provenance**. Never blend tiers into one opaque score.

```
Tier 1  oracle:test-exec   real evaluation (FAIL_TO_PASS via darwin bench/eval,
                           executed on a remote GPU host over SSH) — GROUND TRUTH
Tier 2  judge:fable        headless Fable LLM-as-judge (ADR-172) — smarter proxy
Tier 3  proxy:structural   output-verifier structural confidence — WEAKEST, triage only
```

## [issue:strands-agents/harness-sdk#1659] (issue) [FEATURE] MCP Specification 2026-07-28 adoption (parent tracker)#1659
https://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk/issues/1659
# [FEATURE] MCP Specification 2026-07-28 adoption (parent tracker)#1659
## Summary
Originally filed for the 2025-11-25 revision; retitled because the **2026-07-28 revision** (RC locked 2026-05-21, final ships 2026-07-28) supersedes it and changes what's worth building. It is the largest revision since MCP launched.

- Deprecated features registry: [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/deprecated](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/deprecated)

## What the 2026-07-28 revision changes
| Change | SEP | Deeplink |
|-|-|-|
| Fully stateless protocol: initialize handshake, `Mcp-Session-Id` sessions, SSE resumability (`Last-Event-ID`), and `ping` **removed**; version/clientInfo/capabilities ride in `_meta`; `server/discover` replaces the handshake | SEP-2575, SEP-2567 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/lifecycle](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/lifecycle) |
| MRTR (multi round-trip requests) replaces server-initiated `sampling/createMessage`, `elicitation/create`, `roots/list` | SEP-2322 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/utilities/mrtr](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/basic/utilities/mrtr) |
| Notifications consolidated into `subscriptions/listen` (one long-lived stream; opt-in `toolsListChanged`, `promptsListChanged`, `resourcesListChanged`, `resourceSubscriptions`) | SEP-2575 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/changelog) |
| Tasks move from core to a redesigned official extension: polling `tasks/get`, new `tasks/update` for mid-flight input, unsolicited task handles (`resultType: "task"`), `input_required` state, `tasks/list` removed | SEP-2663 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/tasks/overview](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/tasks/overview) |
| **Deprecated** (12-month window): sampling, roots, MCP logging (`logging/setLevel` removed; direction is stderr + OTel) | SEP-2577 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/deprecated](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/deprecated) |
| Tool schemas loosened to full JSON Schema 2020-12; `structuredContent` may be any JSON value | SEP-2106 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/changelog) |
| List caching (`ttlMs`/`cacheScope`) on tools/prompts/resources list results | SEP-2549 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/changelog) |
| Auth: CIMD recommended registration (finalized 2025-11-25); dynamic client registration deprecated; incremental scopes; Enterprise-Managed Auth (XAA) extension stable 2026-06-18 | SEP-991, SEP-835 | [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization) · [https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/enterprise-managed-auth/](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/enterprise-managed-auth/) |

Both SDKs delegate wire mechanics to the official MCP libraries (Python `mcp>=1.23,<2` currently negotiates through 2025-11-25; TS `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.25.2`), so the base protocol lands via dependency bumps to the 2026-07-28-capable releases. The strands-side work is unwinding assumptions: Python's long-lived-session/daemon-thread lifecycle, TS's connect state machine and old-stream listChanged wiring, and both tasks implementations (built against the 2025-11-25 core utility being replaced by the extension).

## [pull_request:openobserve/openobserve#13527] (pull_request) Design at: [#13526](https://github.com/openobserve/openobserve/issues/13526)
https://github.com/openobserve/openobserve/issues/13527
## Summary
Implements MCP specification revision **2026-07-28** (stateless protocol) alongside the existing 2025-11-25 behavior on the same endpoint, following the spec's dual-era server model: requests carrying modern per-request `_meta` are served per 2026-07-28, while `initialize` selects legacy semantics.

## Changes
- **Version negotiation** (`src/api/http/.../mcp/mod.rs`, `src/mcp/src/protocol.rs`): the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header is now validated against a supported-version set (`2026-07-28`, `2025-11-25`) instead of strict equality — the old check would have rejected every client that upgrades to the new revision. Unsupported versions (header or body `_meta`) get `400` + JSON-RPC `-32022` (`UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`) listing the supported versions so clients can retry.
- **`server/discover`** (`src/mcp/src/protocol.rs`): new RPC required by 2026-07-28, returning `supportedVersions`, `capabilities`, server identity in `_meta`, `instructions`, and `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` cache fields.
- **Modern result decoration** (`src/mcp/src/protocol.rs`): requests declaring `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion: 2026-07-28` in `_meta` get `resultType: "complete"` and `_meta` server identity on results, plus `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` on `tools/list`. Legacy responses carry none of these fields — byte-for-byte unchanged.
- **Request metadata headers** (`src/api/http/.../mcp/mod.rs`): modern requests must mirror body fields into `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` headers (including the Base64 sentinel encoding for `Mcp-Name`); missing or mismatched headers are rejected with `400` + JSON-RPC `-32020` (`HeaderMismatch`), per the transport's server-validation rules.
- **HTTP status mapping**: unknown methods on modern requests return `404` + `-32601` so dual-era clients can distinguish a modern server from a legacy one; version errors return `400`. Legacy requests keep errors in-band with `200` as before.
- **Legacy paths untouched**: `initialize`, `ping`, the GET SSE keepalive channel, DELETE no-op, and notification → `202` handling are unchanged.

## Testing

## [doc:https://agentgateway.dev/blog/2026-08-03-new-mcp-spec-revision/] (doc) Agentgateway out the gate with support for the 2026-07-28 MCP specification with release of version 1.4
# Agentgateway out the gate with support for the 2026-07-28 MCP specification with release of version 1.4
The latest revision of the MCP specification -- `2026-07-28` -- is finally out.

There are plenty of resources out there talking about the new revision. One that I came across a couple of weeks ago is An MCP Tool Call Deconstructed, which I'm sure you'll enjoy.

One thing is undeniable: the people involved in bringing about this new revision have not been idle.

## The new spec, briefly
In a nutshell, the protocol is no longer stateful. This change does away with a litany of issues relating to handling state. With the new specification, we no longer worry about directing clients to sticky server instances to maintain state.

We no longer see MCP session IDs accompanying requests and responses, and clients no longer open with an `initialize` method call.

The new revision formalizes three MCP extensions: MCP Apps, Tasks, and Enterprise Managed Authorization.

Version 2 of the MCP Inspector is out, and with it come some nice improvements.

## Agentgateway version 1.4
Agentgateway v1.4 was released on July 27, one day before the release of the `2026-07-28` revision of the MCP spec. One of version 1.4's biggest themes is support for the new revision of the specification. Version 1.4.1 has already been released, only 2 days later, providing increased compatibility with the new revision.

## Try out the examples
As of the time of this writing, that particular MCP server has not yet been ported to the new revision of the spec.

MCP Apps have been with us for a few months already, but with the release of the `2026-07-28` revision, the MCP Apps extension is explicitly graduated. But you can also try it out with the new "v2" MCP inspector, which also supports MCP Apps.

## [doc:https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/mcp-stateless/] (doc) MCP Goes Stateless: What the 2026-07-28 Spec Changes and How to Migrate
# MCP Goes Stateless: What the 2026-07-28 Spec Changes and How to Migrate
###### Contents
The Model Context Protocol is the open standard that connects LLM clients to tools, data, and services, and until recently every MCP connection carried a session.

The 2026-07-28 specification removes all of that. It is the largest revision of MCP since launch, and its headline is a stateless protocol core: **the initialize handshake is gone, the session id is gone, and every request now stands on its own.** The old 2025-11-25 spec keeps working, and a new deprecation policy guarantees at least a twelve-month overlap, so this is a migration you can plan rather than scramble through.

## The 2026-07-28 spec: a stateless core
### Removing the handshake and sessions
As a side effect, the list endpoints (`tools/list`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list`) no longer vary per connection.

### A request, before and after

## Migrating
### Deprecations to know
Several features are deprecated alongside sessions. Roots, Sampling, and Logging are deprecated via SEP-2577; they still work and will keep working for at least twelve months, but new implementations should not adopt them, and the server-initiated versions of sampling, elicitation, and roots listing are now handled through Multi Round-Trip Requests instead. On the authorization side, the spec hardens security (including RFC 9207 issuer validation) and formally deprecates Dynamic Client Registration in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents, again with backward compatibility during the transition.

## Core MCP 2026-07-28 Lifecycle

The current core revision has no `initialize` handshake or `Mcp-Session-Id`. Each request includes its protocol version, client identity, and client capabilities. Servers implement `server/discover` for optional up-front capability discovery, and clients can retry with a supported version when needed.

This change does not remove the MCP Apps View's separate `ui/initialize` handshake. Read MCP 2026-07-28 for MCP Apps before updating a server or SDK.

## What Can Servers Expose?

MCP defines three types of capabilities that servers can expose:

- **Tools** — Functions the model can call. Used for actions like fetching data, running computations, or modifying state.
- **Resources** — Data the model can read. Identified by URIs with MIME types. Used for structured data, files, and (in MCP Apps) interactive HTML UIs.
- **Prompts** — Reusable prompt templates. Not currently used by MCP Apps.

Protocol revision **`2026-07-28`** shipped on 28 July 2026. It is the largest breaking change since MCP launched, and since #259 already moves us onto SDK v2 this is the natural release to absorb it.

No client has shipped it yet — Anthropic's connector docs still cap at `2025-11-25` and VS Code at `2025-06-18` — so the target is: **write against SDK v2, serve both eras on the wire** via `createMcpHandler` with the default `legacy: 'stateless'`. This is not a cutover, it is dual-era support.

## What changes for us
| Change | Impact here |
|-|-|
| Stateless core; `initialize`/`notifications/initialized` handshake and `Mcp-Session-Id` removed | Anything cross-call becomes an explicit server-minted handle passed as a tool argument |
| `tools/list` MUST NOT vary per-connection (may vary by the auth on the request) | Any capability-gated registration must key off per-request auth, not connection state |
| New mandatory `server/discover` RPC | Returns supported protocol versions, capabilities, identity |
| **MRTR replaces all server-initiated requests** | `elicitation/create` as a server-initiated call is gone — see #341 |
| `resultType` (`"complete"` | `"input_required"`) required on every result | Pre-2026 results treated as `"complete"` |
| `ttlMs` + `cacheScope` (`public`/`private`) required on `tools/list`, `prompts/list`, `resources/list`, `resources/read`, `resources/templates/list` | We currently emit neither |
| Tools SHOULD be returned in deterministic order | Prompt-cache surface; worth pinning by test |
| `subscriptions/listen` replaces the HTTP GET endpoint and `resources/subscribe` | Not used today |
| `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` headers required on Streamable HTTP POSTs | Relevant to #303 |
| Removed: `ping`, `logging/setLevel`, SSE resumability / `Last-Event-ID` | — |
| Schema loosened to any JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords | Already on 2020-12 via the SDK v2 emitter |

# MCP 2026-07-28 stateless compatibility

Research date: 2026-08-09.

## Contract and primary sources

MCP revision `2026-07-28` changes Streamable HTTP from a protocol-session
model to a per-request model. Modern clients do not call `initialize` or
`notifications/initialized`, and the server does not mint `Mcp-Session-Id`.
Every JSON-RPC message uses a separate HTTP POST and carries protocol version,
client identity, and capabilities in request metadata.

Primary sources:

- MCP 2026-07-28 changelog
- Streamable HTTP specification
- SEP-2575: Make MCP Stateless
- OpenAI Codex support commit
- Official OpenAI MCP documentation

Required modern request fields include:

- `MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28`
- `Mcp-Method: <json-rpc-method>`
- `Mcp-Name: <tool-name>` for `tools/call`
- matching `params._meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"]`
- per-request client capabilities and, preferably, client information

Kaneo validates the bearer token before protocol routing on every request.
Modern requests use a fresh `McpServer` instance and hold no process-local
protocol state. Requests classified as the 2025 era continue through the
existing sessionful transport, preserving `initialize`,
`notifications/initialized`, and `Mcp-Session-Id` behavior.

This dual-era split matters: treating a sessionful `2025-06-18` exchange as
"stateless" because its POSTs use separate TCP connections does not implement
the `2026-07-28` contract.

# MCP: support spec revision 2026-07-28 (stateless protocol, dual-era server)\#13526

New issue

New issue

Assignees

Milestone

v0.92.0

## Description

hengfeiyang

## Background

MCP specification revision **2026-07-28** was published, making the protocol fully stateless:

- The `initialize`/`notifications/initialized` handshake and the `Mcp-Session-Id` header are removed. Protocol version, client info, and client capabilities now travel in `_meta` on every request (`io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, etc.).
- A new `server/discover` RPC is **required** (servers MUST implement it) to advertise supported versions, capabilities, and identity.
- All results must carry a `resultType` field (`"complete"` / `"input_required"`).
- List results (`tools/list`, etc.) must carry `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` cache-control fields.
- Streamable HTTP POSTs must carry `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` headers that mirror body fields; servers that process the body MUST validate header-body consistency and reject mismatches with `400` \+ JSON-RPC error `-32020` (`HeaderMismatch`).
- Unsupported protocol versions must be rejected with `400` \+ JSON-RPC error `-32022` (`UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`) listing supported versions.
- Unknown methods on modern requests must return HTTP `404` with JSON-RPC `-32601`.

Spec: [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)

# Introducing the Terminal-Bench Dataset Registry with SWE-Bench Verified, AppWorld, DevEval, and EvoEval

An easy way to evaluate agents on popular benchmarks and distribute new benchmarks to agent developers.

Today we’re announcing the Terminal-Bench registry: an easy way to evaluate agents on many agentic benchmarks via the Terminal-Bench framework. For benchmark developers, the Terminal-Bench registry also offers a way to distribute benchmarks to agent developers and run existing agents in a unified way.

Terminal-Bench-Core, our benchmark for evaluating agents in the command line, provides a comprehensive testbed for measuring agents on software engineering, scientific computing, system administration, and more. But benchmarks from other researchers, like SWE-Bench, AppWorld, DevEval, etc. help paint a broader picture of agent performance on specific domains.

Until now, evaluating agents on multiple benchmarks has been difficult and time-consuming. Each benchmark comes with its own repository, evaluation harness, dependencies, and Docker images. Testing a new agent or model means cloning each of these repositories and spending hours or days familiarizing yourself with the project's structure and getting it to run.

The Terminal-Bench registry solves this problem. Benchmark developers can now build new benchmarks using—or adapt existing ones to use—the Terminal-Bench harness, which provides logging, live streaming, popular agent integrations, parallelization, distribution via Terminal-Bench CLI, and, coming soon, cloud hosting out of the box.

To supplement the launch of the Terminal-Bench registry, we’ve adapted four popular benchmarks into the Terminal-Bench framework and registered them on the Terminal-Bench registry.

| Benchmark | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **SWE-Bench Verified** | A well-known benchmark for evaluating LLMs on real-world software issues collected from GitHub. Given a codebase and an issue, a language model is tasked with generating a patch that resolves the described problem. |
| **AppWorld** | A suite of natural, diverse, and challenging autonomous agent tasks requiring rich and interactive code generation. It focuses on practical, multi-step operations that require interaction with various tools and APIs to achieve a goal. |
| **DevEval** | A benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs across various stages of the repo-level software development lifecycle, including software design, environment setup, implementation, acceptance testing, and unit testing. |
| **EvoEval** | "A program synthesis benchmark suite created by evolving existing benchmarks into different targeted domains for a comprehensive evaluation of LLM coding abilities." |

The Terminal-Bench registry enables agent developers to integrate their agent into Terminal-Bench once and immediately start evaluating their agent on registered evals or even start building their own set of domain-specific in-house evals.

# Swarm

OpenAI's Swarm is an experimental framework designed to facilitate lightweight and ergonomic orchestration of multi-agent systems. It introduces two primary abstractions: **Agents**, which encompass specific instructions and tools, and **handoffs**, enabling agents to transfer control to one another. This design allows for scalable and testable coordination among multiple AI agents, each specializing in distinct tasks, to collaboratively achieve complex objectives.

In recent developments, OpenAI has released the **Agents SDK**, a production-ready evolution of the Swarm framework. The Agents SDK builds upon the foundational concepts introduced in Swarm, offering enhanced features for orchestrating the workflow of multiple AI agents. This advancement enables developers to manage and coordinate complex tasks more effectively, ensuring that various agents work harmoniously towards unified goals.

Therefore, the recently released OpenAI Agents SDK is indeed based on the design patterns and principles initially explored in the Swarm framework, marking a significant step towards more sophisticated and integrated multi-agent AI systems.

OpenAI's Swarm is an experimental framework designed to facilitate the orchestration of multi-agent systems in an ergonomic and lightweight manner. It introduces two primary abstractions: **Agents** and **handoffs**.

**Agents** are autonomous entities equipped with specific instructions and tools to perform designated tasks. Each agent operates independently, focusing on its assigned role, which enhances specialization and efficiency within the system. For example, in a customer service application, separate agents could handle billing inquiries, technical support, and general information requests.

**Handoffs** refer to the mechanism by which control and context are transferred from one agent to another. This allows the system to dynamically route tasks to the most appropriate agent based on the current context or user request. For instance, if a general inquiry agent identifies a billing-related question, it can hand off the conversation to the billing agent, ensuring that the user's query is addressed by the most qualified entity.

The Swarm framework emphasizes a minimalist approach, focusing on simplicity and flexibility. This design makes it accessible for developers to experiment with multi-agent orchestration without the complexity often associated with more extensive frameworks. By leveraging these core abstractions, Swarm enables the creation of scalable, testable, and efficient multi-agent systems capable of handling complex, collaborative tasks.

## 1. Orchestration Patterns

### Pattern Taxonomy

| Pattern | Topology | Control Flow | Best For |
|---------|----------|-------------|----------|
| Fan-out/Fan-in | Star | Central coordinator dispatches parallel tasks, aggregates results | Independent subtasks (research, search, validation) |
| Pipeline (Sequential) | Linear | Each stage processes and passes to next | Document processing, multi-stage reasoning |
| Supervisor/Worker | Hierarchical | Supervisor delegates, monitors, collects | Structured workflows with clear task decomposition |
| Swarm/Mesh | Decentralized | Agents hand off directly to peers based on capability | Open-ended tasks, customer support routing |
| Hierarchical Delegation | Tree | Multi-level supervisors, each managing sub-teams | Complex enterprise workflows with specialization |

### Framework Implementations

**Fan-out/Fan-in:**
- AutoGen v0.4: ConcurrentOrchestration via AgentChat layer; agents work in parallel with results collected by runtime
- LangGraph: Parallel branches in graph with fan-in node; state merging at convergence point
- Semantic Kernel: ConcurrentOrchestration pattern (experimental) — agents process same input independently, results aggregated
- CrewAI: Parallel task execution within Flows; Crew tasks can run concurrently when no dependencies exist

**Pipeline:**
- AutoGen v0.4: Sequential pattern — linear task flow, each agent builds on previous output
- LangGraph: Linear graph edges, each node is an agent step
- Semantic Kernel: SequentialOrchestration — agents process in turn, output becomes next input
- CrewAI: Sequential process within a Crew; tasks execute in defined order

- LangGraph: `langgraph-supervisor-py` library; supervisor uses tool-calling to delegate to sub-agents. Recent recommendation: use tool-calling approach directly rather than specialized libraries for better context engineering control

https://github.com/railwayapp/cli/issues/885
## Summary

Comprehensive rewrite of the CLI's `caller` detection. Replaces the old single-pass env/`ps`-walk with a six-layer pipeline and routes JSON-RPC `clientInfo` from `railway mcp` tool events into the telemetry payload so MCP-driven calls get tagged authoritatively from the handshake.

Validated live against 11 agent harnesses (Claude Code CLI/Desktop, Claude-in-Cursor-terminal, Cursor agent mode, OpenCode, Amp, Codex CLI/Desktop, Pi, Copilot CLI, Factory Droid). 11/11 detected correctly. Factory Droid is the canonical case the old detector would have leaked into `agent_subprocess`.

Pairs with railwayapp/dbt-analytics#128 which normalizes the new caller taxonomy in `fct_agentic_events` / `dim_agent_session`.

## What changed

### Detection pipeline (`src/telemetry.rs`)

Six layers, evaluated in order — first match wins:

1. **`RAILWAY_CALLER` env override** (existing, unchanged)
2. **Strong agent env signals** — `CLAUDECODE`, `CURSOR_AGENT`, `CODEX_SANDBOX`, `OPENCODE`, `AMP_CURRENT_THREAD_ID`, `PI_CODING_AGENT`, `__COG_BASHRC_SOURCED` (Devin), `AI_AGENT`, `COPILOT_CLI`, `AIDER`, `FACTORY_DROID`, `GEMINI_CLI`, `REPLIT_AGENT`. Includes a fix for a typo where the old code looked for `CLAUDECODE_SESSION_ID` (doesn't exist) instead of `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`.
3. **Process-tree walk** — single `ps -A` snapshot (replaces N per-hop spawns) parsed into a `HashMap`, walks up to 15 ancestors. Matches against full argv (catches node-bundled agents like `node /path/cursor-agent`) plus exact-basename matching for short generic names (`droid`, `pi`, `amp`).
4. **AI-IDE host detection** — `__CFBundleIdentifier` (Cursor `com.todesktop.230313mzl4w4u92`, Windsurf, VS Code, Claude Desktop, JetBrains, Zed), `TERM_PROGRAM`, `TERMINAL_EMULATOR=JetBrains-JediTerm`. Combined with `isatty(stdout)` to disambiguate human vs subprocess in the same IDE: `tty:cursor` vs `agent_unknown:cursor`.
5. **Cloud-IDE / sandbox env** — `REPL_ID`, `CODESPACES`, `CLOUD_SHELL`, `MONOSPACE_ENV` (Firebase Studio), `ANTIGRAVITY_CLI_ALIAS`.
6. **CI provider** — `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `GITLAB_CI`, `CIRCLECI`, `BUILDKITE`, `JENKINS_URL`, `TRAVIS`, `TF_BUILD`, `CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID`, `NETLIFY`, `VERCEL`, `RAILWAY_*`, etc.
7. **Bucketed fallback** — interactive shell with no IDE → `tty`. Non-interactive subprocess buckets by parent interpreter (`agent_unknown:python`, `agent_unknown:node`, `agent_unknown:shell`, `agent_unknown:ruby`, ...) so even unidentified harnesses give us a useful axis.

### MCP `clientInfo` is now authoritative for MCP events

`src/commands/mcp/handler.rs` snapshots `context.peer.peer_info().client_info` and threads it into a new `send_mcp_tool_with_client`. The clientInfo name (per the MCP JSON-RPC spec, every client must send it during `initialize`) maps to the canonical caller value:

Coding agent products (IDEs, CLIs, full suites)

### What is the harness?

Atlarix is a desktop coding agent whose harness owns the full tool-call loop for open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax) plus BYOK and local Ollama/LM Studio. Approvals, waits, background commands, and sub-agent delegation are enforced by the harness rather than the prompt, so a weaker model cannot emit a premature completion; in Build/Debug modes the agent runs the project's own checks (tsc/eslint/ruff/pytest) through a per-OS write-confining sandbox (Linux Landlock, Windows AppContainer, macOS Seatbelt) and cannot declare a task done while those checks fail. The Electron desktop UI is the shell.

## Why Most AI Agents Fail Before the Job Is Done
Building a long-running AI agent that works autonomously for hours — completing dozens of subtasks, recovering from errors, staying on track — is an entirely different challenge.

## Component 2: Persistent Memory and State Management
A long-running AI agent will almost certainly exceed the context window of any current model if it tries to keep everything in memory at once.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### What is a long-running AI agent?
A long-running AI agent is an autonomous AI system designed to execute complex, multi-step tasks over an extended period — minutes to hours — without continuous human oversight. Unlike simple prompt-response interactions, these agents plan, use tools, track progress, handle errors, and adapt their approach to complete a goal that involves many interdependent actions.

### How is a long-running agent different from a regular AI workflow?
A standard workflow follows a fixed sequence of steps. A long-running agent is adaptive — it can make decisions, replan when things go wrong, and take different paths based on what it encounters. Workflows are predictable; agents are flexible.

### Do long-running agents require multi-agent systems?
Not always.

## Key Takeaways
- Long-running agent failures are almost always architectural, not model quality issues.

# Question on Training Efficiency and API Cost Compared to Standard RL\#399

## Description

l-besiege-l

Last edited by l-besiege-l

Hello, thanks for open-sourcing this great project! I have a question regarding the training efficiency of ART with RULER:

1. How does the time efficiency compare to standard reinforcement learning approaches? Specifically, how many training steps (on average) are typically required for convergence when using RULER as opposed to a hand-crafted reward function?

2. What is the approximate API cost of training an agent with RULER, considering that it requires repeated LLM calls for reward evaluation? For example, does it scale linearly with rollout length and number of trajectories, or are there optimizations in place to reduce cost?

Understanding these aspects would be very helpful for deciding whether to adopt ART with RULER for production-level tasks. If you could also share a paper or related reference material, I would greatly appreciate it.

Thanks in advance!

Hi, @l-besiege-l,

1: RULER is most useful when you don’t have ground truth and can’t build a handcrafted reward function that you can trust. If you do know the correct function, a handcrafted one will usually be more efficient. That said, it is a but more nuanced. RULER evaluates not just the final result but also intermediary steps, which can make it more efficient. You’ll need to test it on your specific use case to know what works better.

2\. RULER calls the judge model once per trajectory group. A rough formula for cost is:

`price per token * avg. trajectory tokens * (trajectories per group + judge output tokens) * groups per step * training steps`

Your judge inference provider may cache repetitive tokens.

Again, easiest way to know for sure it run a training job for a few steps and see the inference cost.

# Harbor (Terminal Bench)

Harbor lets you evaluate a pydantic-deep agent on Terminal-Bench — the benchmark that scores agents on real, end-to-end terminal tasks inside isolated containers.

This is a small reference adapter. It plugs the pydantic-deep CLI into Harbor's installed-agent interface so the benchmark can install, run, and score your agent without you writing any glue.

## What it does

The adapter is a single class, `PydanticDeepAgent`, that implements Harbor's `BaseInstalledAgent`. Harbor drives it through three phases for every task:

1. **Install** — spins up a fresh container, installs `uv`, creates a virtualenv at `/opt/pydantic-deep-venv`, and `pip install`s `pydantic-deep[cli]` straight from the GitHub repo.
2. **Run** — invokes `pydantic-deep run` in **headless mode** (`--json --verbose`) with the task instruction, forwarding your API keys into the container.
3. **Post-run** — parses the agent's stdout for token usage and USD cost and reports them back to Harbor.

You bring a model and your API keys; the adapter handles the rest.

## Run an evaluation

The adapter's module docstring documents the entrypoint. Point Harbor at it with `--agent-import-path`:

```console
$ harbor run -d "terminal-bench@2.0" \
    -m anthropic/claude-opus-4-6 \
    --agent-import-path apps.harbor.agent:PydanticDeepAgent
```

That's the whole loop: Harbor pulls the Terminal-Bench dataset, builds a container per task, installs pydantic-deep, runs it against each instruction, and scores the result.

!!! note "Model names are converted for you"
    Harbor passes models as `provider/model`. The adapter rewrites them to
    pydantic-ai's `provider:model` form — so `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6`
    becomes `anthropic:claude-opus-4-6`. A bare name or one that already uses
    `:` is passed through unchanged.

## Aim

Measure PraisonAI agent performance — specifically the **`praisonai code`** terminal-native code assistant — on **Terminal-Bench 2.1** via the official **Harbor** harness, so the project has a real, repeatable score (like Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenHands on the leaderboard). Everything lives in the **examples/benchmark layer + CI** — deliberately **no changes to `praisonaiagents` core or the published SDK surface**.

## Current state (validated against real Harbor source, not docs)

The repo **already contains** an integration at `examples/terminal_bench/` (external/wrapper/installed adapters, 4 test files, 3 job YAMLs, README) — but a line-by-line review against Harbor `main` (`laude-institute/harbor`, v0.16.x: `src/harbor/agents/base.py`, `agents/installed/base.py`, `models/agent/context.py`, `models/job/config.py`, `cli/jobs.py`, `agents/factory.py`) found it is **not runnable today**, has **never been run in CI**, has **no recorded scores**, and **never invokes `praisonai code`**:

**A. Broken adapter plumbing (bugs):**

1. `praisonai_external_agent.py:79` — reads `getattr(context, 'env', {})`; `AgentContext` has **no `env` field** (only `n_input_tokens, n_cache_tokens, n_output_tokens, cost_usd, rollout_details, metadata`). `--ae` keys arrive via the `BaseAgent.extra_env` property → **API keys are never injected**; every LLM call fails unless keys pre-exist on the host.
2. `praisonai_installed_agent.py:275` — reads nonexistent `context._last_stdout`; and its in-container runner (`:180-190`) reads `agent._usage`/`agent._cost`, **neither exists** in praisonaiagents (the real accessor is the `cost_summary` property dict) → metrics are never populated. `run()` (`:232-238`) discards the `ExecResult` stdout entirely.
3. `praisonai_wrapper_agent.py:206-212` — calls `environment.exec_as_root`, which **doesn't exist on `BaseEnvironment`** (it's a `BaseInstalledAgent` method); falls back to `sudo` (absent in TB task containers). Correct: `environment.exec(command=..., user="root")`.
4. `praisonai_external_agent.py:187` — gates `cost_summary` behind `callable(...)`; it's a **property returning a dict**, so the gate always fails (works only by accident via private attrs).
5. `praisonai_installed_agent.py:34-55` — silent MagicMock stubs on ImportError mask a dead integration; mock `CliFlag` field name (`name`) differs from the real dataclass (`kwarg`).

**B. Job configs silently do nothing:**

6\. All three YAMLs use `dataset:` / `agent:` / `n_concurrent:` / `task_filter:` — the real `JobConfig` schema is `datasets: [{name, version, task_names}]`, `agents: [{import_path, model_name, env, kwargs}]`, `n_concurrent_trials`, `n_attempts`. Unknown keys are **silently ignored by pydantic → the job runs the default oracle agent on zero datasets.**

7\. `job.yaml` contains multiple `---` YAML documents → `yaml.safe_load` raises `ComposerError`; `harbor run -c job.yaml` dies at parse.

8\. Dataset id drift: configs pin `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2` (2.0); **Terminal-Bench 2.1 is current** (published 2026-04-30; 26 tasks fixed incl. reward-hacking robustness) — official run form: `harbor run -d terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1 …` ( tbench.ai docs). `--agent-import-path` is deprecated+hidden; current CLI accepts the import path via `--agent "module:Class"`.

9\. `job_test_5.yaml` task names (`hello-world`, `fix-permissions`, …) are unverified against the actual task registry.

**C. Tests are largely aspirational:**`test_integration.py` uses relative imports in a directory with **no `__init__.py`** → `ImportError` is swallowed as `pytest.skip("Harbor not installed")` **even when Harbor is installed**; constructors omit the required `logs_dir`; it patches `praisonaiagents.approval.set_approval_backend`, which doesn't exist; `pytest-asyncio` never declared. `test_basic.py` mocks all Harbor modules (validates imports only). `test_agent_comparison.py` runs tasks on the **host**, not in containers.

**D. `praisonai code` is never benchmarked.** The wrapper adapter shells out to bare `praisonai "TASK"` (auto/agents-generator mode, no shell-tool loop); external/installed variants instantiate `Agent()` directly. Meanwhile `praisonai code` **is headless-capable today, with zero SDK changes**: one-shot mode exists (`cli/commands/code.py:153-158`), and `--dangerously-skip-approval` (or `--no-safe`) sets `PRAISON_APPROVAL_MODE=auto` \+ `PRAISONAI_TOOL_SAFETY=off` (`code.py:88-96`), which both empties the non-TTY `_perm_deny` preset (`agent/agent.py:1926-1976`) and installs the auto-approve callback (`main.py:7104-7114`) → fully autonomous in a container, no hang. Official repository: [https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor)

- **Core Function**: Supports evaluation of various Agents (Terminus-2, Claude Code, OpenHands, etc.)
- **Core Innovation**:
  - Multiple environment support (Docker, Daytona, E2B, Modal)
  - Parallel execution and resume capability
  - Automatic evaluation and result analysis
- **Core Objective**: Evaluate agents' comprehensive capabilities in **task completion, tool usage, and policy compliance**

### 2. Supported Features

1. **Multi-Agent Support**
   - Built-in Agents: terminus-2, claude-code, openhands, aider, codex, etc.
   - Custom Agents: via `--agent-import-path`

2. **Multi-Environment Support**
   - Docker (local)
   - Daytona (cloud)
   - E2B (sandbox)
   - Modal (cloud)

3. **Dataset Support**
   - Local path: `-p /path/to/dataset`
   - Remote dataset: `-d dataset-name@version`

### 3. Core Evaluation Mechanism

- **Automatic verification**: Evaluate results via verifier
- **Parallel execution**: Control concurrency via `-n/--n-concurrent`
- **Resume capability**: Detect existing results, skip completed tasks
- **Trace export**: Export traces via `--export-traces`

# Harbor Framework Overview

## What It Is
Harbor is "a framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench for evaluating and optimizing agents and language models." It enables evaluation of agents like Claude Code and OpenHands, creation of custom benchmarks, parallel experimentation across thousands of environments, and rollout generation for reinforcement learning.

## License & Metrics
- **License:** Apache-2.0
- **Stars:** 5,000
- **Latest Release:** Information not provided in the page content

## Supported Agents
The documentation mentions Claude Code and references support for "arbitrary agents like Claude Code, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and more," though specific complete listings aren't detailed.

## Supported Datasets & Environments
**Datasets:** Terminal-Bench-2.0, SWE-Bench, and Aider Polyglot (via `harbor datasets list`)

**Environments:** Docker (local), Daytona, Modal, LangSmith, Blaxel, Novita Sandbox, and Tensorlake

## Advanced Features
The page does not explicitly mention resume capabilities, trace export functionality, or pass@k metric support.

## Maintainers
Maintained by "the Harbor Framework Team" according to the citation information provided.

# Terminal-Bench Challenges Overview

**What It Is:**
Terminal-Bench Challenges are "long-horizon, token-intensive, single-task benchmarks" designed to evaluate agents completing substantial projects autonomously. Unlike shorter benchmarks, these tasks simulate work that would typically require teams of experts months to complete.

**Publication Timing:**
The article does not specify an exact publication date, though it references the initial Terminal-Bench release and notes this represents a new benchmark format.

**What It Measures:**
The benchmarks assess agent capability to independently manage large-scale development projects, including correctness and task-specific performance metrics. Tasks involve no time or resource constraints, allowing agents to work until completion.

**Task Details:**

- **Number:** Three challenges released initially
- **Duration:** Days per task (compared to hours for previous Terminal-Bench formats)
- **Grading:** Task-specific metrics measuring correctness and performance
- **Solution scope:** Approximately 10,000-500,000 lines of code

**The Three Challenges:**
1. Rust Compiler Speedup (optimization)
2. Inference Engine Codegolf (C/CUDA implementation under 25kb)
3. WASM WebGL Renderer (JavaScript/WebAssembly graphics renderer)

**Reported Results:**
Agents tested with 12-hour runs showed limited success: marginal progress on compiler optimization, incomplete correctness matching on inference tasks, and approximately 50% test coverage on WebGL (96.4% on WebGL 1.0, 20.5% on WebGL 2.0).

# GitHub sweep, 1 June to 7 September 2026

Source: repository pages, raw files, release pages, vendor changelogs and developer search. Every number below carries its URL. Where a figure exists only in a secondary roundup I say so; where a project publishes a claim it cannot substantiate I say that too.

---

## 1. The tool bridge moved under us: MCP 2026-07-28

The single most consequential change in the window for `packages/mcp` is the [MCP 2026-07-28 revision](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog), the largest since MCP launched. The protocol is now stateless: the `initialize` handshake and `Mcp-Session-Id` are gone, protocol version and client capabilities ride in per-request `_meta`, a mandatory `server/discover` RPC replaces the handshake, every result carries `resultType`, and list results carry `ttlMs`/`cacheScope`. Streamable HTTP POSTs must carry `Mcp-Method`/`Mcp-Name` headers that servers validate against the body. MRTR (multi round-trip requests) replaces server-initiated `sampling/createMessage`, `elicitation/create` and `roots/list`; sampling, roots and MCP logging are deprecated on a twelve-month window; tool schemas loosen to full JSON Schema 2020-12.

The migration pattern the ecosystem settled on is **dual-era, not cutover**. [OpenObserve's implementation](https://github.com/openobserve/openobserve/issues/13527) serves 2026-07-28 for requests carrying modern `_meta` and 2025-11-25 for anything that calls `initialize`, byte-for-byte unchanged. [Agentgateway shipped v1.4 on 27 July](https://agentgateway.dev/blog/2026-08-03-new-mcp-spec-revision/), one day before the spec. A [Kaneo design note dated 9 August](https://github.com/usekaneo/kaneo/blob/main/apps/docs/core/integrations/mcp-stateless.mdx) makes the point that matters for us: treating a sessionful 2025-06-18 exchange as "stateless" because its POSTs use separate TCP connections does not implement the contract. Notably, [as of a mid-window tracker](https://github.com/stumason/coolify-mcp/issues/337), no major client had shipped the revision — Anthropic's connector docs still capped at 2025-11-25 — so servers are ahead of clients.

For us this is mostly good news. Statelessness pushes cross-call state into explicit server-minted handles passed as tool arguments, which is closer to our session log than MCP sessions ever were. The work is real but bounded: a `server/discover` responder, `resultType` and cache fields on our outbound tool lists, and a decision about MRTR before elicitation's deprecation window closes.

## 2. Vendor harnesses: convergence, and one shutdown

Claude Code continued near-daily releases to [2.1.263](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md), with `bashOutputMaxChars`/`taskOutputMaxChars` raising inline output limits to 128K, `--append-subagent-system-prompt-file` for large subagent prompts, and `/skill-doctor` reporting unused skills and their context cost. The 2.1.180+ range is where the convergence with our seams is visible: `SendMessage`/`ListAgents` for cross-session agent communication, agent definitions carrying `model:`/`permissionMode:`, `PreModelSwitch`/`PostModelSwitch` hooks that can block or annotate, network sandboxing with domain allowlisting, worktree isolation, and `/goal` for background task monitoring. Codex CLI shipped [0.153.0 through 0.153.4 on 3-4 September](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases) with plugin-marketplace management, app-server reconnection and MCP tool approvals scoped to app accounts; 0.147.0 earlier in the window brought portable Agent Plugins across local, personal, workspace and remote sources plus an opt-in 2026-07-28 MCP implementation.

The window's hard lesson is Google's. [Google announced](https://developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli/) that on **18 June 2026** Gemini CLI and the Code Assist IDE extensions stop serving requests for Pro, Ultra and free individual tiers, which move to Antigravity CLI (`agy`), a closed-source Go binary. Enterprise licences and paid API keys continue. Secondary reporting describes the retired repository as Apache-2.0 with roughly 104k stars and about 6,000 external contributors. An open-source harness with a vendor behind it stopped serving requests on a date — that is the argument for model-agnosticism, made better than we could make it ourselves.

[OpenHands shipped roughly ten releases](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/releases) between 30 July and 27 August, moving toward a managed product: automation run phases, an automations catalog, LLM pre-flight validation that rejects misconfigured profiles before a run, per-run cost tracking, a "ready-for-dev" issue readiness gate, and MCP enable/disable with disabled skills excluded from agent context. The pre-flight validation is the piece worth stealing: a fleet cell with a misconfigured route should fail at plan freeze, not mid-shift.

On the closed side, [Amp had a dense July](https://ampcode.com/news): agent-to-agent spawning and file exchange (17th), subscriptions (18th), the Puck meta-agent and Slack (20th), **self-scheduling agents that "set their own schedules, wake themselves up, and keep working" (21st)**, Multiplayer (22nd), and **event-driven Orbs that react to CI failures, Linear issues, monitor alerts or any HTTP request (23rd)**, then Global Plugins and Skills (11 August). That is a commercial always-on product shipped three months before we have one. A [secondary catalogue](https://github.com/bradagi/awesome-cli-coding-agents) puts Factory Droid top of Terminal-Bench with headless CI mode, and Cursor CLI's Cloud Handoff (`&` prefix moves a live session to a cloud agent) as the cleanest answer to leaving a long task running.

## 3. The field, ranked, and the upstream we forked

A [star-ranked survey pulled from the GitHub API on 29 August](https://pinggy.io/blog/best_open_source_cli_coding_agents/) gives the shape of the open field: OpenCode ~202k (MIT), **DeepSeek Harness ~203k (MIT)**, Codex CLI ~119k (Apache-2.0), Pi ~98k, OpenHands ~85k, Cline ~67k, Goose ~54k (now under the Linux Foundation), Aider ~48k with no commits since May 2026, then CodeWhale, Continue, Reasonix, Crush, Qwen Code, Kilo Code and Grok Build. All licence and star figures there are from one secondary source. The structural point is that model labs stopped outsourcing the terminal.

[The upstream itself](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) confirms MIT, developer-preview status and roughly 214.7k stars over about 15,210 commits when read on 7 September. Two consequences for Daliesk: our fork carries `improvement/`, `verification/`, `components/` and `governance/` groups upstream does not, so merge cost is a standing line item; and the harness alone is not the moat, because a 214k-star MIT version of it exists.

Three open-weight coding flagships landed inside the window, all from [one secondary roundup](https://pinggy.io/blog/best_open_source_self_hosted_llms_for_coding/) and none independently verified here: Qwen3.8-Max weights published 14 August under Apache-2.0 (reported 67.7 SWE-Bench Pro, 86.6 Terminal-Bench 2.1, text-only, 262K context); GLM-5.3 announced 14 August with weights held two weeks for a safety review and published 29 August under a bespoke licence; DeepSeek V4-Flash GA on 31 July and V4-Pro build 0813 on 13 August at 1.6T total / 49B active, with the API moving to peak/off-peak pricing on 16 August. A bespoke per-model licence and time-of-day pricing are both things our curator terms and budget policy do not currently model.

## 4. RL infrastructure and environment hubs

Prime Intellect had the strongest window. The single most consequential change in the window for `packages/mcp` is the [MCP 2026-07-28 revision](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog), the largest since MCP launched. The protocol is now stateless: the `initialize` handshake and `Mcp-Session-Id` are gone, protocol version and client capabilities ride in per-request `_meta`, a mandatory `server/discover` RPC replaces the handshake, every result carries `resultType`, and list results carry `ttlMs`/`cacheScope`. Streamable HTTP POSTs must carry `Mcp-Method`/`Mcp-Name` headers that servers validate against the body. MRTR (multi round-trip requests) replaces server-initiated `sampling/createMessage`, `elicitation/create` and `roots/list`; sampling, roots and MCP logging are deprecated on a twelve-month window; tool schemas loosen to full JSON Schema 2020-12.

The migration pattern the ecosystem settled on is **dual-era, not cutover**. [OpenObserve's implementation](https://github.com/openobserve/openobserve/issues/13527) serves 2026-07-28 for requests carrying modern `_meta` and 2025-11-25 for anything that calls `initialize`, byte-for-byte unchanged. [Agentgateway shipped v1.4 on 27 July](https://agentgateway.dev/blog/2026-08-03-new-mcp-spec-revision/), one day before the spec. A [Kaneo design note dated 9 August](https://github.com/usekaneo/kaneo/blob/main/apps/docs/core/integrations/mcp-stateless.mdx) makes the point that matters for us: treating a sessionful 2025-06-18 exchange as "stateless" because its POSTs use separate TCP connections does not implement the contract. Notably, [as of a mid-window tracker](https://github.com/stumason/coolify-mcp/issues/337), no major client had shipped the revision — Anthropic's connector docs still capped at 2025-11-25 — so servers are ahead of clients.

For us this is mostly good news. Statelessness pushes cross-call state into explicit server-minted handles passed as tool arguments, which is closer to our session log than MCP sessions ever were. The work is real but bounded: a `server/discover` responder, `resultType` and cache fields on our outbound tool lists, and a decision about MRTR before elicitation's deprecation window closes.

# ruflo vs the Daliesk harness: an engineering comparison

Read against `ruvnet/ruflo` at commit `277c7bc03ad192eef6d6f57e59ab7bab69a5728d` (5 September 2026, a shallow clone at `/home/user/ruvnet/ruflo`) and `deepseek-harness` at `/home/user/deepseek-harness`. Where I could not verify something from code or a primary page, I say so.

## 1. What ruflo actually is

Ruflo is not a harness in our sense. Its own coordination rule is explicit: *"MUST spawn concurrent agents using Claude Code's Task tool. Never use MCP tools alone for execution — Task tool agents do the actual work"* (`CLAUDE.md:86-88`). Claude Code owns the agent loop, the tool pipeline, the context window and the permission model. Ruflo is a decoration layer around it: an MCP server of coordination tools, a set of hooks, a memory store, a plugin marketplace and a daemon. The README calls this an "agent meta-harness for Claude Code and Codex", which is accurate.

**Architecture.** The npm package is still `claude-flow` at version `3.38.21` (`package.json`). The tree is a pnpm/npm workspace under `v3/@claude-flow/` with about 25 sub-packages (`cli`, `swarm`, `memory`, `providers`, `neural`, `security`, `mcp`, `guidance`, `shared`, `embeddings`, `plugin-agent-federation`, and others), plus 40 directories under `plugins/` distributed as Claude Code plugins through `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, plus a `crates` symlink to `v3/crates` for Rust. 2,153 TypeScript files, 1,884 Markdown files, 563 test files.

**Swarm and hive-mind.** `v3/@claude-flow/swarm/src/` holds `queen-coordinator.ts` (a "Central Orchestrator for 15-Agent Swarm" doing task analysis, capability-scored delegation, health monitoring and consensus), `topology-manager.ts`, `unified-coordinator.ts`, `agent-pool.ts`, `message-bus.ts`, `attention-coordinator.ts`, and `consensus/` with `raft.ts`, `byzantine.ts` and `gossip.ts`. This is a real coordination library. What it coordinates, though, is Claude Code Task-tool spawns; the actual execution path where a child is really launched is `spawn('claude', ['--print','--output-format','json'], …)` in `v3/@claude-flow/cli/src/services/headless-worker-executor.ts:1397` and `spawn('claude', argv, …)` in `services/fable-harness.ts:210`. The queen's "consensus" runs over coordinator state, not over model output that gates anything.

**Memory.** `v3/@claude-flow/memory/src/` is the largest single subsystem: `agentdb-backend.ts` (`class AgentDBBackend extends EventEmitter implements IMemoryBackend`), `hnsw-index.ts`, `hybrid-backend.ts`, `fts5.ts`, `memory-graph.ts`, `consolidator.ts`, `persistent-sona.ts`, `learning-bridge.ts`, `entity-tagger.ts`. The `agentdb.rvf` file at the repository root is a binary container with an `SFVR` magic prefix — RVF, the "RuVector Format", a portable cognitive container for embeddings, metadata and causal graphs (`plugins/ruflo-rvf/README.md`). Encryption at rest is AES-256-GCM behind `CLAUDE_FLOW_ENCRYPT_AT_REST`, off by default; RVF export bytes are not encrypted. This memory store is ruflo's authority for state: it is mutable, embedding-indexed, and consolidated by an LLM-driven `consolidator`.

**The "dream" work.** `docs/dream-cycle/` documents a nightly Routine (`trig_01HpEqAcEP7wzrxy3TzakrQ2`, 06:00 UTC) that researches one "deep" area, opens an issue, and since v2 evaluates a candidate and opens a PR. `LEDGER.md` is a durable cross-night table. It is the most intellectually honest artefact in the repository, and it is damning: the v1 routine from 25 May to 13 August 2026 filed 80 issues, of which **4 shipped (5%), 1 rejected, 75 (94%) never touched**. Under v2, every night from 24 August to 5 September produced an evaluated `ACCEPT`, and every resulting PR (#3086, #3094, #3103, #3110, #3119, #3123, #3130, #3139, #3152, #3160) was still open or draft at the head commit. The ledger also records its own three-times-repeated failure mode: rows reach `main` only by PR merge, so the ledger gets stuck on unmerged branches.

**Plugins and skills.** 35 plugins advertised in the README (40 directories on disk), installed via `/plugin marketplace add ruvnet/ruflo`. 39 skills under `.claude/skills/` and 33 agent definitions under `.claude/agents/`. Both are Claude Code artefacts — Markdown files the vendor product loads — not a runtime registry with identity or lineage. There is a `plugins/ruflo-deepseek-harness/`, but it is only DeepSeek API `chat`/`reason` skills, not an integration with our harness.

**MCP surface.** `v3/@claude-flow/cli/src/mcp-tools/` holds 47 tool modules; a crude count of `name: '…'` registrations gives 309. The README contradicts itself on the total: line 38 says "314 MCP tools", line 256 says "~210 MCP tools". Both cannot be right.

**Models and providers.** `v3/@claude-flow/providers/src/` ships six adapters: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google`, `cohere`, `ollama`, `ruvector`. These serve auxiliary work (embeddings, routing, judging). The agentic path is Claude Code and Codex, i.e. the operator's vendor subscription, which is a genuine strength for cost but means ruflo is not model-agnostic where it matters.

**Verification.** `verification/` is *not* task verification. It is a regression-protection witness system: every documented fix is attested by a SHA-256, a marker substring, and an Ed25519 signature anyone on the same commit can re-derive, in per-OS bundles (`linux/`, `macos/`, `windows/`) with append-only `history.jsonl`, gated by a `witness-verify` CI job that blocks publish. It exists because three May 2026 regressions passed unit tests and broke users on install (`verification/README.md`). It is a good mechanism aimed at a different problem than ours.

**Tests, licence, cadence, maintainers.** 563 test files, but `v3/vitest.config.ts:44-51` has every coverage threshold commented out — *"Coverage thresholds disabled for alpha (London School TDD uses mocks). TODO: Re-enable for stable release."* So there is no coverage gate. MIT (`LICENSE`, "Copyright (c) 2024-2026 ruvnet"). Ten releases between 12 August and 2 September 2026, all patch-level. The GitHub page reports 71.2k stars, 8.4k forks, 648 open issues and 293 open pull requests. The shallow clone shows a single author, `rUv`; the repository's own README notes it "can include community contributions, automation, generated artifacts, and imported history."

## 2. Provenance of the headline claims

**SWE-Bench 84.8%.** Appears in `.claude-plugin/README.md:657`, `.claude-plugin/docs/PLUGIN_SUMMARY.md:162`, `v3/CHANGELOG.md:45` and three `SKILL.md` files. There is no harness, no run artefact, no seed, no date and no model attached to it anywhere in the tree. Ruflo's own `ADR-171:17` states the opposite in plain words: **"ruflo has no SWE-bench oracle"** — historically `resolved` was derived from structural confidence, "a *proxy*". The number is marketing, contradicted by the repository's own architecture decision record.

**32.3% token reduction and 2.8-4.4x WASM speedup.** Same files, same absence of method. Adjacent numbers in the same repository were audited and found fabricated: `docs/reviews/intelligence-system-audit-2026-05-29.md:53` records that the "Flash Attention 2.49x-7.47x" figure was *"Fabricated at runtime: `attention-coordinator.ts:972` → `flashSpeedup = 2.49 + Math.random()*4.98`"*, with the real tiled kernel measuring ~1.1x. `docs/dream-cycle/dream-gist-2026-09-05.md` records that the CLI cold-start benchmark suite produced every number, including a "V2 vs V3 Speedup: 5.00x", from `setTimeout()` chains with no code between them, while a real `measureColdStart()` sat unused in the same file. To ruflo's credit, both were found and corrected by its own loop, and `CLAUDE.md:791` now says the Flash Attention speedup was "dropped to avoid a credibility claim we can't reproduce".

**Stars and downloads.** 71.2k stars is verifiable on the repository page. The README's "Git clones (14d) 106k" badge links to `data/clone-data.ledger.json`, which contains twelve snapshots in which **every repository entry reads `{"count":0,"uniques":0,"error":"fetch-failed"}`**, and `data/clone-data.proof.json` whose latest snapshot headline is *"9.6M npm downloads · 0k git clones (14d)"*. The badge is contradicted by the file it cites. The npm figure (9,561,819 downloads over 12 months, captured 2026-08-14) does have a named source and method.

The pattern is consistent: ruflo's ADRs and audits are careful; its README and plugin metadata are not, and the marketing numbers have outlived the ADRs that refute them.

## 4. Verdict: "it seems like us, but aren't we better?"

Mostly yes, but not for the reasons the pitch usually gives, and not on every axis.

Ruflo and Daliesk are solving different problems that look alike from the README. Ruflo maximises what a Claude Code subscription can be made to do: it adds coordination, memory and a plugin marketplace on top of someone else's loop, and it has real distribution — 71.2k stars, 8.4k forks, 35 installable plugins, roughly 9.6M npm downloads in twelve months. We own the loop, the log and the certificate, and we have no distribution channel of our own. On the criteria a European lab actually sells against — a single authority for state, checks authored before the work, a reward an agent cannot reach, paired-seed experiments, a coverage gate — ruflo has essentially nothing, and its own ADR-171 says so.

**Three things ruflo does better than we do today.**
1. **Distribution.** `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` puts 35 plugins one `/plugin install` away inside the product most of our prospects already run. Our bundles reach nobody who has not cloned the repository.
2. **Signed, per-platform artefact attestation.** `verification/README.md` describes an Ed25519 witness manifest per OS with append-only history and a `witness-verify` CI job that blocks publish. We have executable completion standards for tasks and nothing comparable for released artefacts.
3. **A binding standard for published numbers.** `v3/docs/adr/ADR-169-benchmark-reporting-integrity-standard.md` (3 July 2026) forbids relaxed metrics presented as accuracy, undisclosed best-of-N, no-work passes hidden in aggregates and unreproducible cherry-picks. We have the machinery to satisfy such a rule and no rule.

**Three things we do that ruflo cannot.**
1. **Reconstruct exactly what the model saw.** `docs/architecture.md:97` makes model-visible equal logged, with a runtime invariant. Ruflo's authority is a mutable, LLM-consolidated vector store (`v3/@claude-flow/memory/src/consolidator.ts`); a rewritten memory cannot be replayed.
2. **Gate completion on a certificate the implementer cannot reach.** `packages/verification/README.md` plus `read-barrier/` give a validator-owned tree, per-run reservations and a per-session deny enforced where paths are opened. Ruflo has no barrier and no oracle.
3. **Decide a change with a frozen, paired experiment.** `packages/improvement/experiments/README.md` freezes a plan by content digest, runs two arms at the same repetition indexes and returns a bootstrap interval and a verdict. Ruflo's nightly loop produces one ACCEPT per night from a single evaluated candidate.

**Three things worth adopting from it.**
1. **The witness manifest**, applied to our composition manifest: a signed content address per component per platform, verified before publish (`verification/README.md`).
2. **ADR-169's five reporting rules**, wired into the observatory's render path so an unlabelled or best-of-N figure is unpublishable by construction (`v3/docs/adr/ADR-169-benchmark-reporting-integrity-standard.md`).
3. **The ledger's merge-rate feedback**: v2 reads prior nights' fates first and biases toward real evaluation when the trailing merge rate is zero (`docs/dream-cycle/LEDGER.md`). Our shifts record what they ran; they do not yet record whether anyone used it.

The honest caution is that ruflo's failure mode is one we are exposed to. Its always-on loop produced 80 issues with a 5% ship rate, then ten consecutive certified-good PRs that nobody merged. Certificates raise the quality of a shift's output; they do not create the human capacity to land it. That is a sales and staffing problem, not an architecture problem, and our architecture does not solve it.

Both deliverables are written and validated (`items.json` parses, 31 items, all fields present, dates well-formed).

**Files** (in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-deepseek-harness/f53f80cc-1f77-5d02-a862-99d59ffabdce/scratchpad/research-2026q3/github/`):

**The five that matter most**

1. **MCP 2026-07-28, stateless core** — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog — handshake and session id removed, mandatory `server/discover`, MRTR replaces sampling/elicitation/roots, 12-month deprecations. Servers are ahead of clients, so a dual-era `packages/mcp` costs nothing and loses nothing.
2. **Prime Intellect, Scaling Agentic RL (22 Jul)** — https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/scaling-agentic-rl — ~365k tasks behind one taskset API, plus the validation ritual (no-op must fail, gold patch must pass with 10× retries) and an unusually candid admission that grading inside the agent's sandbox is "mitigation, not a guarantee". Their open problem is our `read-barrier`.
3. **OpenAI retracts SWE-Bench Pro (8 Jul)** — https://openai.com/index/separating-signal-from-noise-coding-evaluations/ — ~30% of 731 public tasks broken; the audit method (pipeline flags 286, then Codex investigators plus five human engineers) is the environment-health check we should run.
4. **verifiers 0.3.0 / prime-rl 0.8.0 multi-agent (7 Aug)** — https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/multi-agent-systems — `Agent.run → Trace`, `Env.run(task, agents)`, and a vocabulary where a *harness* is Claude Code or Codex and an *Agent* is harness × model × runtime. That is our fleet cell; aligning `dsh-trajectory/1` with their `Trace` buys interoperability.
5. **Amp self-scheduling agents and event-driven Orbs (21 and 23 Jul)** — https://ampcode.com/news — a commercial always-on product with external-event wake, shipped before ours. Also worth pairing with https://theaidigest.org/village, running 15+ agents every weekday since 1 Apr 2025 at ~$10k/month with a public dataset.

Honourable mention because it settles our positioning: Google stopped serving Gemini CLI for individual tiers on 18 June 2026 (https://developers.googleblog.com/an-important-update-transitioning-gemini-cli-to-antigravity-cli/) — a ~104k-star Apache-2.0 harness switched off on a date.

**Part B verdict**

Mostly yes, but not for the reasons the pitch usually gives. Ruflo and Daliesk look alike only from the README: ruflo maximises what a Claude Code subscription can be made to do — its own `CLAUDE.md:88` says "Never use MCP tools alone for execution — Task tool agents do the actual work", so Claude Code owns the loop, the context and the permissions, and ruflo adds coordination, memory and a marketplace on top. It has real distribution we lack (71.2k stars, 8.4k forks, 35 installable plugins, ~9.6M npm downloads/12mo). On the criteria a European lab sells against — one authority for state, checks authored before the work, a reward the implementer cannot reach, paired-seed experiments, a coverage gate — ruflo has essentially nothing, and its own ADR-171 says so in as many words ("ruflo has no SWE-bench oracle"), while the 84.8% SWE-Bench, 32.3% token-reduction and 2.8–4.4× WASM figures survive in `.claude-plugin/README.md` with no harness, seed, model or date anywhere in the tree, and its git-clone badge is contradicted by the ledger file it links to (every snapshot `error: "fetch-failed"`, zero clones). Three things it does better: distribution through the Claude Code plugin marketplace; signed per-OS Ed25519 witness manifests with a publish-blocking CI job; and ADR-169, a binding standard for every published number. Three things we do that it cannot: reconstruct exactly what the model saw; gate completion on a certificate behind a validator-owned read barrier; and decide a change with a frozen, paired, bootstrap-interval experiment. Three worth adopting: the witness manifest applied to our composition manifest, ADR-169's five rules wired into the observatory's render path, and the dream-cycle ledger's merge-rate feedback. The caution is real, though — ruflo's always-on loop produced 80 issues at a 5% ship rate, then ten consecutive certified-good PRs nobody merged. Certificates raise the quality of a shift's output; they do not create the human capacity to land it, and our architecture does not solve that.
